added_claim_errors: The 'use the smallest of' formula lists '$7,500 minus any other 2026 IRA contributions' but never compensation minus other contributions. Someone who earns $4,000 and contributes $2,000 gets $4,000 from it, but the correct cap is $2,000.
'The 2026 IRA limit is $7,500 per the IRS' credits the IRS with no link or document number, so the source claim can't be checked (the figure itself is right per IR-2025-111).

'to count for 2026 the money needs to land in the Roth by December 31, 2026 — don't rely on the April 2027 filing deadline' treats December as the legal deadline. Per the 2026 Form 5498 instructions and 219(f)(3), a rollover designated for 2026 can be made through April 15, 2027.
'the 15-year clock restarts for the new beneficiary' presents the beneficiary-change reset as settled. No IRS guidance exists, so the question is unresolved.
'If the annual limit rises with inflation, this compresses to four or five years' is wrong about four: even at $8,000 a year, four years gives only $32,000, short of $35,000, so it still takes five.
'Scholarships ... don't count' as earned income is too broad. From my own knowledge, the SECURE Act (2019) treats taxable non-tuition fellowship and stipend payments as compensation for IRA purposes.
'Most [plans] do [support it] by 2026, but not all' gives no source and can't be checked.

reasons: Both answers correct the premise up front. Both give the $7,500 annual cap, the compensation limit, the $35,000 lifetime cap, the $13,000 that can never move this way, the son-owned Roth, the direct transfer and the state-tax caveat. A gets the deadline right: December is not the federal deadline, and a 2026 rollover can be made through April 15, 2027. It also spells out what happens if all $48,000 moves (6% excise on the Roth side, earnings taxed plus 10% on the 529 side) and stays hedged on the 15-year reset. A's flaw is a subtle gap in its 'smallest of' formula. B treats December 31 as the legal deadline, says the 15-year clock 'restarts' after a beneficiary change as if settled, and wrongly suggests the transfers could take four years. B says rolling all $48,000 would create a 'tax mess' but never states the 6% excise or the 529-side tax. It is also much longer and repeats itself (the CPA question list, the repeated trap sections). B's 1099-Q Box 4b, recipient and Form 5498 Box 10 details check out against the IRS 1099-Q instructions, but that does not make up for these errors.
